title: Mountain Biking in Snowdonia
strapline: From technical downhill at Antur Stiniog to flowy trail centre runs at Coed y Brenin, Snowdonia serves up legendary mountain biking.
metaDescription: Explore Snowdonia's epic mountain biking trails! Find the best routes, gear shops, and insider tips for your adventure.
heroAlt: Mountain biker riding through a forest trail in Snowdonia, with mountains in the background
introduction:
Snowdonia is where mountain biking in the UK was effectively invented as a destination sport. Coed y Brenin, near Dolgellau, opened in 1996 as the UK's first purpose-built mountain bike centre — managed by Forestry Commission Wales (now Natural Resources Wales), it set the template every other British trail centre followed. Thirty years on, the original red routes (MBR, Dragon's Back) and the more recent Temtiwr black are still the benchmark for trail-centre flow. If you've ridden a graded trail anywhere in the UK, the design lineage traces back here.

That heritage anchors a riding scene that now spans four distinct flavours in the same valley system. Trail-centre flow at Coed y Brenin and Beddgelert (signed, graded, well-drained — beginner-friendly through to black). Gravity-fed downhill at Antur Stiniog above Blaenau Ffestiniog, where 14 trails feed off the UK's most-praised uplift service onto slate-spoil tips repurposed into proper bike park terrain. Natural-trail riding at Penmachno — full loops (Dolen Machno, Dolen Eidda) that read more like proper mountain biking than a trail centre: moorland singletrack, technical rocky descents, navigation needed, lower footfall than Coed y Brenin. And the hand-cut Marin Trail in Gwydir Forest near Betws-y-Coed, with the Gwydir Mawr & Bach unsigned loops as the local-knowledge underground option.

What ties the four together is the landscape: long climbs into proper hills, slate-quarry post-industrial backdrops, and weather that turns on you faster than anywhere south of the border. None of this is sanitised. Penmachno can be impassable in winter; Antur Stiniog runs uplift-only in real wet; even Coed y Brenin's reds have lung-buster climbs and rocky chunder that catch out riders expecting a flat blue. Pair the riding with on-site cafés (Beics Brenin at Coed y Brenin, the Antur Stiniog café at the bike park) and the post-ride pub scene around Betws-y-Coed and Capel Curig and you have a multi-day MTB destination on a par with anything in Scotland or the Lakes — with the bonus of a UNESCO-listed slate landscape as the backdrop.

A note on what isn't here: BikePark Wales (often searched alongside Snowdonia) is in the Brecon Beacons, not Eryri — a three-hour drive south. Llandegla (One Planet Adventure) is in the Clwydian Range, just outside the park, and is the standard wet-weather alternative when North Wales is washed out. We've kept those out of the spot list below so this page stays honest about what you can reach from a Snowdonia base in a normal riding day.
topTips: Coed y Brenin's visitor centre café and information desk are currently closed (an NRW cost-saving measure) — trails, car park, and toilets stay open, but the site is unstaffed with no first aid on-site. Beics Brenin bike shop next door is still open for hire, spares, and repairs, so head there if you need help, then refuel at Cross Foxes, Ty Siamas, or Meirion Mill Cafe in Dolgellau instead.
Ride Coed y Brenin's reds midweek if you can — MBR and Dragon's Back both get properly congested on weekends and school holidays, and the pinch points on Dragon's Back's climbs are where queues form.

Antur Stiniog's uplift is booked online and the system closes at 4pm the day before — if you miss it, phone them the next morning and they'll usually slot you in. Book ahead for weekends regardless. Bring spare brake pads: the sustained descents chew through pads fast.

Penmachno is proper natural trail riding, not a manicured trail centre — both Dolen Machno and Dolen Eryri currently have several sections closed for forestry work with volunteer-built diversions in place. Check penmachnobiketrails.org.uk/trail-conditions the morning you ride, since the printed map doesn't reflect live closures.

Signal is patchy across Gwydir Forest and Penmachno — download GPX tracks before you leave accommodation. The Gwydir Mawr & Bach (Dduallt) trails aren't waymarked at all, so a phone with an offline map is close to essential, not optional.

Beddgelert Forest is the honest beginner and family choice — gentler gradients, shared use with walkers, and the village itself (ice cream, cafés) makes a natural finish point. Don't take beginners to Coed y Brenin's reds expecting an easy green-blue warm-up; the site skews intermediate-and-up.
Weather turns fast here — check MWIS as well as the Met Office before committing to an exposed ride like Penmachno or the Marin Trail, where there's little tree cover on the moorland sections.
If you're basing yourself in Betws-y-Coed, Beics Betws can sort hire, repairs, and guided rides in one stop and sits a short ride from both the Marin Trail and the Gwydir Mawr & Bach loops.

firstTimer: Start at Coed y Brenin or Beddgelert Forest before anything else — both are signed trail centres with graded routes, unlike Penmachno or the Gwydir hand-cut trails, which assume you can navigate and ride natural terrain unaided.
Budget for parking everywhere — Coed y Brenin, Beddgelert, and the Gwydir Forest car parks near Betws-y-Coed all charge, and Coed y Brenin's machine is card/RingGo only, no cash.

A full-suspension bike isn't compulsory for the trail centre reds, but bring one (or hire one) if you're planning to ride Dragon's Back, Temtiwr, or anything at Antur Stiniog — hardtails make the rocky descents much harder work.

Pack for four seasons in one ride: waterproof jacket, warm layer, gloves, even in July. Snowdonia's weather changes faster than forecasts update, especially at altitude on the Penmachno and Marin Trail moorland sections.
If you're trying downhill for the first time, Antur Stiniog's uplift trails are graded blue to black — start on the easier blues, and don't be shy about walking a section to scope the line first.

Let someone know your planned route and expected return time, especially on Penmachno or the Gwydir Mawr & Bach — these are quieter, less-supervised trails than the main trail centres, and mobile signal is unreliable.
Bring cash or contactless for the small independent cafés (Meirion Mill, Ty Siamas, Caffi Siabod) — Coed y Brenin's own café is currently closed, so don't plan your day around refuelling there.
Book any uplift or guided sessions ahead of time, particularly for weekends — Antur Stiniog's online system cuts off at 4pm the day before, so last-minute weekday planning is safest.
regular: Ride Coed y Brenin first thing on a weekday — the main car park fills fast on weekends, and with the café gone there's less reason for casual visitors to linger, so trail traffic thins out noticeably by mid-afternoon.

Penmachno and the Gwydir Mawr & Bach trails are the crowd-avoidance play when Coed y Brenin is heaving — far lower footfall, no trail-centre polish, but genuinely rewarding natural riding if you're comfortable navigating.

Check Penmachno's live trail-conditions page before heading out — several named sections on both Dolen Machno and Dolen Eryri are currently closed for forestry work, with diversions marked on-site but not always on the downloadable map.
Antur Stiniog runs uplift-only in genuinely wet weather — if it's tipping down, call ahead rather than driving up, and have Marin Trail or Beddgelert as a lower-consequence backup for the day.

Autumn (September-October) gives the best combination on the black and technical red trails: cooler air for the climbs, tackier ground than midsummer dust, and noticeably fewer riders than school-holiday season.
For a quieter take on Gwydir Forest, park near Llyn Elsi and link into the Gwydir Mawr & Bach loops rather than starting from the busier Marin Trail car parks nearer Betws-y-Coed.

Winter riding is viable on the trail-centre routes but Penmachno's exposed moorland sections and the Gwydir natural trails get genuinely difficult in the wet — save those for drier spells and stick to Coed y Brenin or Beddgelert when the ground's saturated.

The post-ride scene has shifted since Coed y Brenin's café closed — Cross Foxes and Ty Siamas in Dolgellau, and Caffi Siabod in Capel Curig for anyone finishing near Beddgelert or Penmachno, are the better bets now rather than assuming the visitor centre will have you covered.

spots.name: MBR Trail, Coed y Brenin
spots.description: The classic MBR trail is a great introduction to Coed y Brenin. It's a flowing red route with berms, rollers, and some technical rock features to keep you on your toes. Expect a good workout with some steady climbs, but nothing too brutal. The views from the top are worth the effort.
spots.bestFor: Intermediate riders looking for a challenging but rewarding trail centre experience.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or anyone with limited mountain biking experience.
spots.bestSeason: Year-round, but can be muddy in winter.
spots.parking: Main Coed y Brenin visitor centre car park. Pay and display. Can get very busy, especially on weekends and school holidays. Arrive early or consider parking at the minor visitor centre closer to Dolgellau and riding in.
spots.insiderTip: Ride it midweek to avoid the crowds, and check out the Beics Brenin cafe for a post-ride coffee and cake.
spots.howToDoIt: Pick up the MBR waymarkers (red) from the visitor centre car park — the route climbs steadily out through forestry tracks before dropping into its first singletrack sections. Ride it clockwise as signed; the climbs are graded to warm you up gradually before the technical descending starts. Expect to stop and read a couple of rock-garden entries before committing on a first lap — most riders walk one or two features the first time through and ride them clean by lap two.
spots.routeDescription: A red-graded loop built around a long, steady climb through mixed forestry followed by several distinct descending sections, each with its own character — flowing berm-and-roller singletrack, a rockier technical section lower down, and a final fast run back toward the car park. It's the trail most people ride first at Coed y Brenin, and it's designed that way: nothing on MBR is a surprise if you're paying attention, but the cumulative climbing adds up.

spots.name: Dragon's Back, Coed y Brenin
spots.description: A longer and more demanding red route than the MBR trail, the Dragon's Back throws in some challenging climbs and technical descents. Expect rocky sections, tight switchbacks, and some exposure in places. It's a rewarding ride for experienced mountain bikers.
spots.bestFor: Experienced intermediate riders looking for a longer and more challenging trail centre ride.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or anyone with limited fitness.
spots.bestSeason: Year-round, but can be muddy in winter.
spots.parking: Main Coed y Brenin visitor centre car park.
spots.insiderTip: The climb up to the 'Dragon's Back' is a lung-buster, so pace yourself. Bring plenty of water and snacks.
spots.howToDoIt: Follow the red waymarkers from the visitor centre — this shares its opening sections with MBR before splitting off onto its own, longer loop. Treat the ride as two halves: a long climbing phase where the goal is pacing, not speed, followed by a sustained descending phase where fitness in your arms and grip strength matter as much as your legs. Riders who've done MBR first usually find Dragon's Back a natural step up rather than a shock.
spots.routeDescription: The longest red at Coed y Brenin, built around a genuinely tough sustained climb — the section riders nickname the lung-buster — that gains height steadily rather than in short sharp ramps. What follows is a long technical descent through rocky, root-laced singletrack with tight switchbacks and a couple of exposed traverses. It rewards riders who've built some fitness on the shorter reds first; going in cold, it can feel relentless rather than fun.

spots.name: Antur Stiniog Downhill Trails
spots.description: Antur Stiniog is a downhill mountain biking mecca. Six trails, graded from blue to black, offer a variety of challenges for all skill levels. Expect steep, technical descents, jumps, drops, and berms. Uplift service available.
spots.duration: Varies depending on number of runs. Allow a full day.
spots.bestFor: Downhill mountain bikers of all skill levels, from experienced riders to those looking to try downhill for the first time.
spots.notSuitableFor: Those who aren't comfortable with steep, technical descents and jumps.
spots.insiderTip: Book your uplift in advance, especially on weekends. Bring spare brake pads – you'll need them!
spots.howToDoIt: Book your uplift slot online before you arrive — the booking system closes at 4pm the day before, so same-day walk-ups aren't guaranteed a place. On arrival, check in at the base, load your bike onto the uplift vehicle, and ride the graded trails down from the top of the old slate workings. Start on a blue to get a feel for the terrain and the uplift rhythm before dropping into red or black runs; the slate-spoil surface rides very differently from forest singletrack and rewards a session-it approach — several runs down the same trail rather than one attempt at the hardest line.
spots.access: Uplift is a paid, booked service, not open trail access — you need a valid pass to use the vehicle, and trails are only legally rideable as part of the uplift operation. In sustained wet weather Antur Stiniog can run uplift-only (no pedal-up access) or curtail runs, so it's worth calling ahead if the forecast is bad rather than turning up on spec.
spots.routeDescription: Multiple graded downhill lines dropping off the slate-quarry spoil tips above Blaenau Ffestiniog, ranging from flowing blue runs with berms and rollers through to technical black lines with rock gardens, drops, and steeper gradients. The post-industrial slate terrain gives the trails a distinctive hardpack, sometimes loose-over-hard character that's different from anything else in this list — good grip when dry, but demanding when wet.

spots.name: Penmachno Trails - Dolen Machno
spots.description: Penmachno offers a more natural and less-ridden experience than Coed y Brenin. Dolen Machno (the shorter loop) is a red-graded route that winds through forests and over moorland. Expect technical climbs, rocky descents, and stunning views. Less 'trail centre', more 'proper mountain biking'.
spots.bestFor: Experienced riders who enjoy a more natural and challenging ride.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or those who prefer flowy trail centre trails.
spots.bestSeason: Year-round, but can be very exposed in bad weather.
spots.parking: Small car park at the trailhead. Free. Can fill up quickly.
spots.insiderTip: The trails can be difficult to follow in places, so download a GPX track to your phone or GPS device. The cafe in Penmachno village is a great place to refuel.
spots.howToDoIt: Download the GPX or route map from penmachnobiketrails.org.uk before you set off — waymarking is sparser than a Forestry-run trail centre, and the route mixes forest track climbs with genuine moorland singletrack where the line isn't always obvious. Check the trail-conditions page the morning you ride: several named sections are currently closed for forestry work with volunteer-marked diversions, so a route loaded the week before may not match what's on the ground.
spots.access: The trailhead car park is small and unstaffed; it fills quickly on good-weather weekends, so have a backup plan (or arrive early) if it's full. The trails cross open moorland in places with minimal shelter, so treat access as weather-dependent — this is not a ride to start into deteriorating conditions.
spots.routeDescription: The shorter of Penmachno's two loops, mixing forestry track climbs with natural, unsanitised singletrack across moorland and through mixed woodland. Expect technical, rooty and rocky sections that demand line choice rather than flow, plus some genuinely exposed stretches with big views back over the Machno and Conwy valleys. It reads much more like proper mountain biking than a groomed trail centre — the trade-off for the lower footfall and rawer riding is that you're more on your own if something goes wrong.

spots.name: Marin Trail, Gwydir Forest, Betws-y-Coed
spots.description: The Marin Trail is a classic mountain biking route in Gwydir Forest. It's a red-graded trail that features a mix of climbs, descents, and technical sections. Expect rocky gardens, tight switchbacks, and some fast, flowing sections. Great views over the Conwy Valley.
spots.bestFor: Experienced intermediate riders looking for a challenging and rewarding ride.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or anyone with limited fitness.
spots.bestSeason: Year-round, but can be muddy in winter.
spots.parking: Several car parks available near Betws-y-Coed. Pay and display.
spots.insiderTip: The climbs are tough, but the descents are worth it. Pack a puncture repair kit, as the trails are rocky in places.
spots.howToDoIt: Park at one of the Gwydir Forest car parks near Betws-y-Coed and follow the red waymarkers for the Marin Trail loop — the route works its way up through forestry before opening onto rockier, more exposed sections with the Conwy Valley views. Pace the sustained climbs conservatively; the descents are where the trail rewards saved energy, with fast, flowing sections interspersed with tight, technical rock gardens that need full attention.
spots.routeDescription: A red-graded loop through Gwydir Forest combining forestry-track climbing with a strong mix of natural and shaped descending — rock gardens, switchback singletrack, and some fast, open sections with views over the Conwy Valley. One of North Wales's original hand-built trails, and it shows in the variety: no two descents feel quite the same.

spots.name: Temtiwr Trail, Coed y Brenin
spots.description: A black-graded trail at Coed y Brenin designed to challenge experienced riders. Expect steep, technical descents, rock gardens, jumps, and drops. Not for the faint-hearted! Requires a high level of skill and fitness.
spots.bestFor: Experienced and skilled mountain bikers looking for a technical challenge.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners, intermediate riders, or anyone not comfortable with steep drops and technical features.
spots.bestSeason: Year-round, but can be very slippery in wet conditions.
spots.parking: Main Coed y Brenin visitor centre car park.
spots.insiderTip: Walk the key sections before you ride them to scope out the best lines. Bring spare brake pads and plenty of confidence.
spots.howToDoIt: Only ride Temtiwr once you're comfortable on Coed y Brenin's reds — it's signed black for a reason. Ride to the top of the main descent and walk the key rock gardens and drop sections first if you haven't ridden it before; there's no shame in scoping a line rather than committing blind. Once you know the trail, session the hardest features individually rather than trying to link the whole thing clean on a first attempt.
spots.routeDescription: A short but intense black descent built to test riders who've already got the trail centre reds dialled — steep chutes, rock gardens, consecutive drops, and technical roll-downs with very little flat recovery between features. It's shorter than MBR or Dragon's Back but demands full concentration throughout; this is not a trail to ride tired or distracted.

spots.name: Beddgelert Forest Trails
spots.description: Beddgelert Forest offers a mix of blue and red-graded trails, suitable for families and intermediate riders. Expect flowing singletrack, gentle climbs, and scenic views. A great option for a less challenging ride in a beautiful setting. Some trails are shared with walkers.
spots.distance: Varies depending on the chosen route.
spots.bestFor: Families, beginners, and intermediate riders looking for a less challenging ride.
spots.notSuitableFor: Experienced riders looking for technical trails.
spots.bestSeason: Year-round, but can be muddy in winter.
spots.parking: Car park at Beddgelert Forest. Pay and display.
spots.insiderTip: Check the trail map before you set off, as some trails are not well signposted. The nearby village of Beddgelert is a charming place to grab a post-ride ice cream.
spots.howToDoIt: Pick up a trail map at the car park before you set off — signage is lighter here than at Coed y Brenin, and the blue and red loops share junctions in places. Beginners and families should stick to the waymarked blue sections; the reds add climbing and technical features that suit riders with some trail-centre experience already. It's a shared-use forest, so expect walkers on some sections and ride with that in mind.
spots.routeDescription: A network of blue and red loops through Beddgelert Forest, with the blues offering gentle, flowing singletrack and forgiving climbs suited to families and newer riders, and the reds adding more technical features and sustained climbing for intermediate riders. The scenery — forest opening onto views toward the Moelwynion — is some of the most approachable in this list, and the short ride into Beddgelert village afterwards makes it an easy half-day out.

spots.name: Gwydir Mawr & Bach Trails (The Dduallt Trails)
spots.description: Hidden amongst the Gwydir Forest, these trails offer a proper mountain bike adventure away from the crowds. Think natural, rooty and rocky singletrack through dense forest. The Dduallt trail itself is a short but challenging loop, great for linking up with other natural trails in the area. This is not a trail centre; navigation skills are a must.
spots.bestFor: Experienced mountain bikers who enjoy natural trails and technical riding.
spots.notSuitableFor: Beginners or those expecting manicured trail centre surfaces.
spots.bestSeason: Year-round, but can be very slippery in wet conditions. Best avoided after heavy rain.
spots.parking: Limited parking available at various points off the minor roads through Gwydir Forest. Parking at Llyn Elsi and cycling up is a good option.

startPoint.name: Parking near Llyn Elsi (starting point suggestion)

spots.insiderTip: Download a detailed map or GPX file onto your GPS device or phone. Signal can be patchy. Be prepared for hike-a-bike sections!
spots.howToDoIt: This is unsigned, so load a GPX track before you leave — don't rely on live signal once you're in the forest. Parking near Llyn Elsi and riding up into the network is the recommended approach; from there you're linking natural singletrack by feel and by map rather than following waymarkers. Go in expecting some hike-a-bike on the steeper or more overgrown sections, and treat it as an exploratory ride rather than a fixed route.
spots.access: There's no formal trailhead — parking is limited to pull-ins along minor forest roads, with the Llyn Elsi car park suggested as the most reliable starting option. Because these are informal, volunteer-maintained lines rather than an official trail centre, access can change with forestry operations; there's no live conditions page to check in advance the way there is for Penmachno, so factor in some uncertainty.
spots.routeDescription: An interlinked network of natural, rooty and rocky singletrack hidden through Gwydir Forest, with the short Dduallt loop as the core route and plenty of scope to extend it by linking in other unsigned trails nearby. Expect dense forest, technical natural features rather than shaped ones, and a genuine sense of exploration — this is the local-knowledge alternative for riders who've done the Marin Trail and want something rawer.

practicalInfo.weather: Snowdonia's weather is notoriously unpredictable. Conditions can change rapidly, even in summer. Be prepared for rain, wind, and sun, and always check the forecast before you set off. Mountain biking can be particularly dangerous in wet or icy conditions, so consider postponing your ride if the weather is poor.
gearChecklist: Mountain bike – a full-suspension bike is recommended for more challenging trails.
Waterproof jacket – even if the forecast is good, be prepared for rain.
Warm layers – temperatures can drop quickly, especially at higher altitudes.
Gloves – to protect your hands and keep them warm.
Puncture repair kit – including spare tubes, pump, and tyre levers.
First aid kit – for dealing with minor injuries.

gettingThere.publicTransport: Nearest train stations are Betws-y-Coed (for Gwydir Forest), Blaenau Ffestiniog (for Antur Stiniog), and Dolgellau (for Coed y Brenin). Bus services connect these towns to other parts of Snowdonia. The Snowdon Sherpa bus service is useful for accessing trailheads.
gettingThere.parkingTips: Parking can be limited at popular trailheads, especially on weekends. Arrive early or consider using public transport. Be aware of parking charges and restrictions.

practicalInfo.safety: Mountain biking in Snowdonia can be challenging, so be aware of the risks. Ride within your abilities, wear appropriate safety gear, and check the weather forecast before you set off. Let someone know your route and estimated return time. In case of emergency, call 999 or 112 and ask for Mountain Rescue. Be aware of livestock on some trails.

faqs.question: What's the best mountain biking area in Snowdonia for beginners?
faqs.answer: Beddgelert Forest is a good starting point, with blue-graded trails suitable for beginners and families. Coed y Brenin also has some easier green and blue trails.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to ride at Antur Stiniog?
faqs.answer: The uplift service at Antur Stiniog typically costs around £42 for a full day (prices can vary). Bike hire is also available at an additional cost.

faqs.question: Are there guided mountain biking tours available in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: Yes, several companies offer guided mountain biking tours in Snowdonia. Plas y Brenin and MUUK Adventures are two well-known options. Guided tours can be a great way to explore the area and improve your skills.

faqs.question: What kind of bike do I need for mountain biking in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: A mountain bike with front suspension is suitable for most trails in Snowdonia. A full-suspension bike is recommended for more challenging routes like the Dragon's Back or trails at Antur Stiniog. Make sure your bike is in good working order before you set off.

faqs.question: Can I ride my e-bike on the mountain bike trails in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: E-bikes are generally permitted on most mountain bike trails in Snowdonia, but it's always best to check with the land owner or trail centre beforehand. Be considerate of other trail users and ride responsibly.

faqs.question: Is it safe to drink the water from streams in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: It's generally not recommended to drink water directly from streams in Snowdonia without treating it first. There is a risk of contamination from livestock and other sources. Carry plenty of water with you or use a water filter or purification tablets.

faqs.question: What are the best months for mountain biking in Snowdonia?
faqs.answer: April to October are generally the best months for mountain biking in Snowdonia, with warmer temperatures and drier conditions. However, the weather can be unpredictable at any time of year, so be prepared for all conditions.

gearShops.description: Bike shop, hire centre, and workshop located at Coed y Brenin Forest Park. They offer a wide range of mountain bikes, clothing, and accessories. They also provide bike servicing and repairs.

gearShops.name: Beics Betws
gearShops.description: Established bike shop in Betws-y-Coed offering bike sales, hire, and repairs. They cater to all levels of mountain bikers, from beginners to experienced riders. They also offer guided rides.

gearShops.name: Antur Stiniog Bike Hire
gearShops.address: Llechwedd Slate Caverns, Blaenau Ffestiniog LL41 3NB
gearShops.description: Bike hire centre located at Antur Stiniog Downhill Centre. They offer a range of downhill bikes to suit all skill levels. Protective gear is also available for hire.

gearShops.name: Summit To Sea
gearShops.description: Based in Llanberis, this shop has everything you need for all things outdoor. Mountain bike parts, spares, clothing and more.

postActivitySpots.name: Cross Foxes
postActivitySpots.description: Popular pub and restaurant located near Coed y Brenin. Known for its hearty meals, good beer, and friendly atmosphere. A great place to refuel after a ride. Excellent for groups.

postActivitySpots.name: Meirion Mill Cafe
postActivitySpots.description: Café known for large portions of homemade cake and traditional dishes, ideal for a post ride treat. Adjacent to a mill shop for a spot of browsing too!

postActivitySpots.name: Y Stablau
postActivitySpots.description: Restaurant and bar in Betws-y-Coed, located in a converted stable block. Offers a wide range of dishes, from pub classics to more sophisticated options. Good selection of beers and wines.

postActivitySpots.name: TY Siamas Cafe
postActivitySpots.description: Welsh culture centre café, serving homemade cakes and light lunches. A relaxed environment for those wanting to sample local culture.

postActivitySpots.name: Caffi Siabod
postActivitySpots.description: Cafe in Capel Curig serving excellent coffee, cakes and light lunches. Perfect for a caffeine fix with stunning views of Tryfan and the Glyderau.

postActivitySpots.name: Hangin' Pizzeria
postActivitySpots.description: Pizza restaurant located in Betws-y-Coed. Fresh pizzas, great for a post bike refuel.

postActivitySpots.name: The Plas Brondanw Gardens & Cafe
postActivitySpots.description: Pleasant cafe within the beautiful Plas Brondanw gardens. Cakes, light snacks, great for the relaxed refuel.

accommodation.name: YHA Coed y Brenin
accommodation.description: Budget-friendly hostel located right in Coed y Brenin Forest Park. A great option for mountain bikers looking for affordable accommodation close to the trails.
accommodation.nearestSpot: Coed y Brenin trails, a few minutes ride

accommodation.name: Tan Dinas Camping & Caravan Park
accommodation.description: Campsite located near Beddgelert Forest. Offers pitches for tents and caravans. A good option for budget-conscious mountain bikers.

accommodation.name: The Royal Oak Hotel
accommodation.description: Located in Betws-y-Coed, this hotel is a short drive from the Marin Trail in Gwydir Forest and the Gwydir Mawr trails. Offers comfortable rooms and a convenient location.

accommodation.name: Plas Gwyn Caravan & Camping Park
accommodation.description: Campsite located near Llanberis offering pitches for tents and caravans. Close to the mountains, this is ideal for a trip up Snowdon too.

accommodation.name: Penmachno Bunkhouse
accommodation.description: Bunkhouse located in Penmachno village, making it a great option for riding the Penmachno trails. With self catering facilities and easy access to the trails it makes for an ideal base.

accommodation.name: Penmaenuchaf Hall Hotel
accommodation.description: A bit of luxury! Situated in a quiet valley near Dolgellau, this hotel is perfect for a bit of pampering after a hard day on the trails. Excellent base for Coed y Brenin.

events.name: Coed y Brenin Enduro
events.description: A popular enduro race held at Coed y Brenin Forest Park. Features a mix of challenging trails and timed stages.

events.name: Welsh Enduro Series
events.description: A series of enduro races held at various locations across Wales, including some in Snowdonia. A great opportunity to test your skills against other riders.

events.description: Downhill race series held regularly at Antur Stiniog.
